relations.text: The Jesuit mission to Asia travelled under the Portuguese Padroado: Xavier sailed at João III's request, and Goa, Malacca and Macau were Padroado sees.
The Catholic monopoly created by the Iberian missions was broken in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries by Protestant and especially Pentecostal growth.

agreements.text: Continued the friars' methods of language study, preaching and inquisition, now with the resources of empire.

disagreements.text: Spanish Dominicans and Franciscans from Manila denounced Jesuit accommodation of Chinese rites to Rome in 1643, opening the Chinese Rites controversy; Spanish friars and Portuguese Jesuits also competed bitterly in Japan.
Portuguese prelates imposed Latin rites and jurisdiction on the East Syriac St Thomas Christians at Diamper (1599), provoking the Coonan Cross revolt of 1653.
English Protestants cited Las Casas's account of Spanish cruelty (the 'Black Legend') to cast their own missions as more humane, while practising dispossession of their own.

deviations: Sublimis Deus (1537) required that the Indians be converted by preaching and good example, yet mission was conducted under conquest, coercion and royal control.
The mendicant ideal of poverty gave way to orders and dioceses holding great estates, slaves and indigenous labour.
Early hopes of a native clergy (Tlatelolco, Kongo's Bishop Henrique) were abandoned for a racially exclusive priesthood.
Royal patronage subordinated the church to the state so thoroughly that Rome itself struggled to direct missions in Iberian territories.

missions.name: Jesuits in Asia (Xavier, Valignano, Ricci, de Nobili, Japan, Chinese Rites)
missions.statusNote: The original Jesuit Asian mission ended with the papal suppression of the Society in 1773, after the Chinese and Malabar rites had been condemned (1715, 1742, 1744) and Christianity proscribed in China (1724) and Japan (1614). The restored Society (1814) returned to Asia under very different conditions, and Rome effectively reversed the rites condemnation in 1939, so the Jesuits' policy of accommodation now shapes Catholic thinking on inculturation.
missions.summary: From Francis Xavier's landing at Goa in 1542 to the suppression of 1773, the Society of Jesus led Catholic mission in Asia under the Portuguese Padroado. Xavier baptised fishing castes in South India and opened Japan; Alessandro Valignano made cultural accommodation official policy; Matteo Ricci won a place at the Ming court as a Confucian-style scholar; Roberto de Nobili lived as a Brahmin sannyasi in Madurai. Japan's Christian community, perhaps 300,000 strong around 1600, was crushed after 1614. In China accommodation of ancestral and Confucian rites became the century-long Chinese Rites controversy, condemned by Rome in 1715 and 1742 and followed by imperial proscription; the Society itself was suppressed in 1773.
missions.story:
The Society of Jesus, approved by Paul III in 1540, was missionary from its foundation, and its members vowed special obedience to the pope regarding missions. At the request of King João III of Portugal, Francis Xavier sailed from Lisbon in April 1541 and reached Goa in May 1542 as papal nuncio. He worked first among the Paravars of the Fishery Coast, a fishing caste who had accepted mass baptism in 1535–37 in return for Portuguese protection against Muslim traders, and then among the Mukkuvas of Travancore, teaching prayers by rote in Tamil translation and baptising, by his own reports, many thousands. He travelled to Malacca, the Moluccas and, after meeting the Japanese fugitive Anjirō at Malacca, to Kagoshima in 1549. Xavier also wrote to João III in 1546 urging that an Inquisition be established in Goa, which was done in 1560. He died on Shangchuan Island off the Chinese coast in December 1552, waiting for passage into China.

Japan became the Jesuits' most spectacular field. Xavier learned that poverty did not impress Japanese elites and adopted fine dress and gifts to win audiences with daimyo. His successors gained the support of lords who wanted Portuguese trade: Ōmura Sumitada became the first Christian daimyo in 1563 and in 1580 ceded Nagasaki to the Society. Alessandro Valignano, visitor of the Asian missions from 1573, insisted that Jesuits learn Japanese etiquette and language, founded seminaries and a college, began training Japanese clergy and sent four young Japanese nobles to Lisbon, Madrid and Rome (the Tenshō embassy, 1582–90). By about 1600 there were perhaps 300,000 Christians. The darker side was real: Christian daimyo such as Ōmura and Arima ordered the destruction of Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines and pressed their vassals and subjects to convert; the Jesuits shared in the profits of the Macau–Nagasaki silk trade; and Portuguese merchants bought Japanese as slaves. In 1587 Toyotomi Hideyoshi, alarmed by Nagasaki's foreign control and by the Jesuit vice-provincial Gaspar Coelho's offers of Portuguese military help, issued an edict expelling missionaries. Rivalry with Spanish Franciscans from Manila, and the San Felipe incident, led to the crucifixion of twenty-six Christians at Nagasaki in 1597. The Tokugawa ban of 1614 began systematic persecution: thousands were executed, many after torture, apostates were registered at Buddhist temples and made to trample images (fumie), and the Shimabara rebellion of 1637–38 ended in massacre. Hidden Christians (Kakure Kirishitan) kept a transformed faith in secret for over two centuries.

In China Valignano sent Michele Ruggieri and Matteo Ricci, who settled at Zhaoqing in 1583. Ricci first wore Buddhist robes, then in 1595 adopted the dress of a Confucian scholar, and presented Christianity as the fulfilment of original Confucianism, criticising Buddhism and Neo-Confucian metaphysics. His world map, his treatises on friendship and memory, his translation with Xu Guangqi of Euclid's Elements (1607) and his catechism Tianzhu shiyi (The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven, 1603) won him admission to Beijing in 1601, where he lived on an imperial stipend until his death in 1610. Converts included the scholar-officials Xu Guangqi, Li Zhizao and Yang Tingyun. After the Ming fell, Johann Adam Schall von Bell directed the Qing Bureau of Astronomy; he was condemned to death in the calendar case of 1664–65 (commuted), but Ferdinand Verbiest restored the Jesuits' position, and the Kangxi Emperor issued an edict of toleration in 1692. Catholics numbered perhaps 200,000 by 1700, many of them in rural communities sustained by Chinese catechists and lay associations rather than by the court.

Ricci had allowed converts to continue honouring ancestors and Confucius, judging these civil rather than religious rites, and used classical terms such as Tian (Heaven) and Shangdi (Lord on High) for God. Spanish Dominicans and Franciscans arriving from Manila, notably Juan Bautista Morales, saw idolatry and appealed to Rome; the Propaganda condemned the practices in 1645, Alexander VII permitted them in 1656 on the Jesuit Martino Martini's representation, and the dispute escalated when the vicar apostolic Charles Maigrot banned the rites in Fujian in 1693. The Jesuits obtained a declaration from Kangxi in 1700 that the rites were civil, which Rome regarded as interference. Clement XI condemned the rites in 1704 and sent the legate Charles-Thomas Maillard de Tournon, whose audiences with Kangxi went badly; Tournon was expelled and died under Portuguese detention in Macau in 1710. The bull Ex illa die (1715) required all missionaries to swear obedience to the ban; Kangxi, reading it, remarked that Westerners could not understand Chinese teaching and it would be better to forbid their preaching. The Yongzheng Emperor proscribed Christianity in 1724, and Benedict XIV's Ex quo singulari (1742) closed debate. Christianity survived in China under persecution, but the opportunity of a court-sanctioned church had passed. In 1939 Pius XII's instruction Plane compertum est permitted Catholics to take part in ceremonies honouring Confucius and ancestors.

In India the Jesuits worked within the Padroado's Latin, Portuguese-speaking church, which was also suppressing the East Syriac heritage of the Thomas Christians; the Jesuit Francisco Ros became their first Latin bishop in 1601 after the Synod of Diamper. Roberto de Nobili, arriving in Madurai in 1606, separated himself from the Portuguese and the low-caste Paravar converts, lived as a vegetarian sannyasi, studied Sanskrit and Tamil, and argued that the sacred thread and caste marks were social signs that Brahmin converts could keep; Gregory XV approved his method in 1623. The Madurai mission later employed 'Brahmin sannyasis' for high castes and 'pandaraswamis' for others, with separate arrangements for Dalits – an accommodation of caste that the Malabar rites decrees of 1704 and 1744 (Omnium sollicitudinum) partly condemned and that left a legacy of segregated Catholic congregations. Jesuits also attended Akbar's court (from 1580), reached Tibet (Tsaparang 1624; Ippolito Desideri in Lhasa 1716–21), and in Vietnam Alexandre de Rhodes helped devise the romanised Vietnamese script (quốc ngữ) and published a catechism in 1651. In Ethiopia Jesuits from Goa secured the conversion of Emperor Susenyos in 1622, but the Latinising policy of Patriarch Afonso Mendes provoked civil war and expulsion in 1633.

European politics ended the mission. Pombal expelled the Jesuits from Portugal and its empire in 1759, France suppressed them in 1764 and Spain in 1767, and under Bourbon pressure Clement XIV dissolved the Society with Dominus ac Redemptor in 1773. Hundreds of Jesuits were shipped home from Asian and American missions; in Beijing the ex-Jesuits continued at court until the Lazarists took over in 1785. Pius VII restored the Society in 1814. Historians now regard the Jesuit Asian mission as both a remarkable intellectual bridge between Europe and Asia and a cautionary case of the costs of elite strategies, colonial entanglement and intra-Catholic rivalry.
beliefs: Post-Tridentine Catholic orthodoxy with a strong emphasis on obedience to the pope and on the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius of Loyola.
Natural theology: reason and the best of non-Christian traditions (especially Confucian ethics) could prepare the way for revelation.
Accommodation (accommodatio): adopting local language, dress, etiquette and permissible customs while preserving doctrine.
Conversion of elites – rulers, daimyo, literati, Brahmins – as the key to reaching whole societies.
The distinction between civil and religious rites, applied to ancestral and Confucian ceremonies and to caste markers.
strategies: Rigorous language study and residence on local terms (Ricci's scholar's robes, de Nobili's sannyasi life).
Science, mathematics, astronomy, cartography and clockwork used to win access to courts.
Christian literature in Chinese, Japanese, Tamil and Vietnamese, including catechisms and apologetics.
Seminaries, colleges and printing presses (the Jesuit mission press in Japan from 1590).
Training of local catechists (dōjuku in Japan) and lay confraternities to sustain communities without priests.
Alliance with the Portuguese crown and trade networks for transport, funding and protection.
groupsReached: Paravar and Mukkuva fishing communities of the Coromandel and Malabar coasts.
Japanese daimyo, samurai and peasants in Kyushu and central Japan.
Chinese scholar-officials and the Ming and Qing courts, and rural communities in Fujian, Jiangnan and Shanxi.
Brahmins and other castes of the Madurai region of Tamil Nadu.
Vietnamese of Tonkin and Cochinchina.
The Mughal court of Akbar and Jahangir, without lasting conversions.
challenges: Persecution by Japanese and Chinese rulers who saw Christianity as foreign and subversive.
Rivalry with Spanish Franciscans and Dominicans and with the French priests of the Missions Étrangères de Paris.
Conflict between the Portuguese Padroado and Rome's vicars apostolic over jurisdiction.
Theological suspicion in Europe that accommodation compromised the faith, culminating in the Rites condemnations.
Few missionaries for vast populations, and long, deadly sea voyages.
The anti-Jesuit politics of Catholic Europe leading to expulsion and suppression.
harms: Christian daimyo, with Jesuit approval, destroyed Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines and pressured subjects to convert; Buddhist monks were expelled from Christian domains.
Jesuits were entangled with Portuguese commerce, profited from the Macau–Nagasaki silk trade, and failed to stop Portuguese slave-trading in Japanese, which Hideyoshi cited in 1587.
Some Jesuits courted military intervention: Gaspar Coelho offered Hideyoshi Portuguese ships and fortified Nagasaki, and Alonso Sánchez proposed a Spanish conquest of China in the 1580s.
Xavier requested an Inquisition for Goa, which from 1560 prosecuted converts suspected of Hindu, Muslim or Jewish practices.
Mass baptisms of Paravars and Mukkuvas with minimal instruction made conversion a matter of caste politics and Portuguese patronage.
Caste accommodation in Madurai institutionalised discrimination against Dalit Christians, including separate seating, churches and priests.
The Rites controversy – a quarrel among European orders – left Chinese Catholics caught between Rome and the emperor and helped provoke the 1724 proscription.
developments: The most sustained intellectual exchange between Europe and East Asia before the nineteenth century, including Western mathematics in China and European knowledge of Confucianism.
Pioneering dictionaries and grammars (the Portuguese-Japanese Vocabulario of 1603, Ricci's romanisation, de Rhodes's Vietnamese dictionary).
The quốc ngữ script, now the standard written form of Vietnamese.
Durable Catholic communities in Tamil Nadu, Vietnam, China and Kyushu, including Japan's Hidden Christians.
A theology of inculturation later endorsed by Vatican II and by the 1939 reversal on Chinese rites.
A native Japanese clergy and the Japanese martyrs, honoured in Nagasaki's Christian heritage (UNESCO, 2018).
missions.outcome: The Jesuits failed to convert the courts of Japan, China or Mughal India, and their Asian mission ended in proscription, persecution and the suppression of the Society; yet they left Catholic communities that survived without missionaries, a corpus of cross-cultural scholarship and a model of accommodation whose questions – how far Christianity may adopt local rites, castes and concepts – remain central to mission.

journeys.text: Waiting for a smuggler to take him to Canton, Xavier died of fever on Shangchuan on 3 December 1552.

journeys.people: Matteo Ricci, Michele Ruggieri and Lazzaro Cattaneo

journeys.people: Roberto de Nobili
journeys.text: After learning Tamil on the Fishery Coast, de Nobili moved to Madurai in November 1606 and adopted the life of a sannyasi.

relations.text: Worked under the Portuguese Padroado, depending on its ships, finances and enclaves (Goa, Malacca, Macau, Nagasaki).

agreements.text: Jesuits used the Xi'an stele, rediscovered c. 1625, to show that Christianity had been honoured in China under the Tang, and like the Jingjiao monks they expressed Christian teaching in Chinese religious vocabulary.
Hudson Taylor's adoption of Chinese dress and residence among the people echoed Ricci's identification with Chinese culture, though for opposite social classes.
Ziegenbalg in Tranquebar, like the Jesuits of Madurai, studied Tamil literature seriously and tolerated caste distinctions in worship to a degree later Protestant missions condemned.

disagreements.text: Spanish Dominicans and Franciscans from Manila attacked Jesuit accommodation of ancestral rites and Confucian terms, taking the Chinese Rites controversy to Rome in 1643.
Jesuit attempts to Latinise the Ethiopian church under Susenyos provoked civil war and the expulsion of 1633.
De Nobili's caste-specific approach anticipated McGavran's 'homogeneous unit principle', which critics in both cases accused of entrenching caste.

deviations: Ignatius's ideal of apostolic poverty and obedience coexisted with Jesuit trading ventures, estates and dependence on Portuguese colonial power.
Accommodation, designed to separate the gospel from European culture, was undermined by the Jesuits' own links to Portuguese empire and by Rome's ultimate rejection of the rites.
Concentration on elites left communities vulnerable when rulers turned hostile, as in Japan after 1587 and China after 1724.
Caste accommodation in Madurai departed from the wider Christian teaching of equality at the Lord's table.

missions.name: Russian Orthodox missions (Stephen of Perm, Innocent of Alaska, Nicholas of Japan)
missions.statusNote: The tsarist missionary system collapsed after 1917, when Soviet persecution destroyed the Imperial Orthodox Missionary Society and most missions. Its daughter churches survived independently: the Orthodox Church in America (autocephalous 1970, with Alaska Native parishes), the autonomous Japanese Orthodox Church (1970), and Orthodox communities in China and Korea. After 1991 the Moscow Patriarchate revived missionary work inside Russia, now closely aligned with the Russian state.
missions.summary: Russian Orthodox mission advanced with the expansion of Muscovy and the Russian Empire across northern Eurasia and into Alaska. At its best it continued the Cyrillo-Methodian tradition of vernacular scripture and liturgy: Stephen of Perm created an alphabet for the Komi in the fourteenth century, Nikolai Ilminsky built native-language schools for the Volga peoples, Innocent Veniaminov translated scripture into Aleut and Tlingit, and Nicholas Kasatkin founded a self-sustaining Japanese Orthodox church. It was also an arm of the state, using tax privileges, legal penalties and force to convert Muslims and animists, and was entangled with colonial exploitation in Siberia and Alaska.
missions.story:
The first great Russian missionary was Stephen of Perm (c. 1340–1396), a monk from Ustyug who learned the language of the Komi (Zyrians) and, in deliberate imitation of Cyril, devised the Old Permic or Abur alphabet in about 1372. From 1379 he preached on the Vychegda river, translated services into Komi and was consecrated first bishop of Perm in 1383. His Life by Epiphanius the Wise celebrates both his translations and his felling of a sacred birch and burning of idols. Monks of the northern Thebaid, inspired by Sergius of Radonezh, carried Christianity to Finnic peoples of the north; Trifon of Pechenga worked among the Sami in the sixteenth century. Stephen's alphabet fell out of use within two centuries, replaced by Church Slavonic and Russian.

When Ivan IV conquered Kazan in 1552 mission became an instrument of empire over Muslim and animist peoples. Archbishop Gurii of Kazan (1555) was instructed to win converts gently, but mosques were destroyed and baptised Tatars ('Kryashens') were given privileges. In the eighteenth century the Office for the Affairs of New Converts (1731/1740–1764) offered converts exemption from taxes and military recruitment – shifting the burden to unbaptised neighbours – while churches replaced mosques; under Bishop Luka Konashevich of Kazan hundreds of mosques were demolished, and there were mass baptisms of Chuvash, Mari, Udmurt and Mordvins who often understood little of the faith. In Siberia Metropolitan Filofei Leshchinsky of Tobolsk (1702–1721) baptised tens of thousands of Khanty and Mansi, burning their sacred images. Apostasy from Orthodoxy was a criminal offence until the 1905 edict of toleration, after which tens of thousands of baptised Tatars returned openly to Islam.

The nineteenth century brought reform. Makary Glukharev founded the Altai mission in 1830, insisting on long instruction before baptism and on translation; he also began a translation of the Old Testament into modern Russian. Nikolai Ilminsky (1822–1891), a Kazan orientalist, developed a system of schools teaching in the mother tongues of the Volga peoples using Cyrillic alphabets, with native teachers and clergy trained at the Kazan Central Baptised-Tatar School (1863) and Teachers' Seminary (1872). Ilminsky's aim was to bind non-Russians to Orthodoxy and the empire before Islam or nationalism could claim them; Russian nationalists attacked it for slowing Russification, and Tatar Muslims for its proselytism, but it gave Chuvash, Mari, Udmurt and others their first literature. The Imperial Orthodox Missionary Society was founded in 1870 under Metropolitan Innocent.

In 1794 eight monks from Valaam reached Kodiak in Russian America at the invitation of the merchant Grigory Shelikhov, whose company had massacred Alutiiq people at Awa'uq (Refuge Rock) in 1784. The monks protested the Russian-American Company's abuse of Native hunters and hostages; Hieromonk Juvenaly was killed around 1796, and the monk Herman lived on Spruce Island until 1837, defending Aleuts and running an orphanage. The priest Ioann Veniaminov arrived at Unalaska in 1824, built a church with Aleut labour, devised an Aleut alphabet with the chief Ivan Pankov and wrote the first Aleut book, Indication of the Way into the Kingdom of Heaven (1833, printed 1840). At Sitka from 1834 he learned Tlingit, and in 1840, as the widowed monk Innocent, he became bishop of Kamchatka, the Kurils and the Aleutians, later serving as metropolitan of Moscow (1868–1879). Orthodoxy took deep root among Aleuts, Alutiiq and Yupik, partly because clergy and Native readers ran schools in Native languages. After the sale of Alaska to the United States in 1867, American policy under the Presbyterian Sheldon Jackson suppressed Native languages in schools, while the Orthodox church remained a refuge of Native identity.

In Japan, Ivan Kasatkin (Nicholas) arrived at Hakodate in 1861 as chaplain to the Russian consulate, studied Japanese language and literature for years, and baptised his first converts, including the former samurai and Shinto priest Sawabe Takuma, secretly in 1868, while Christianity was still banned. Moving to Tokyo in 1872, he relied on Japanese catechists and clergy, translated the liturgy and New Testament with Nakai Tsugumaro, and built the Cathedral of the Resurrection (Nikolai-dō, 1891). During the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) he remained in Japan, praying for its people while ministering to Russian prisoners. At his death in 1912 the church numbered about 33,000. A Russian Ecclesiastical Mission had existed in Beijing since 1715, serving the descendants of Albazin Cossacks and acting as an informal embassy; during the Boxer uprising of 1900 some 222 Chinese Orthodox were killed. A Korean mission opened in 1900.

The revolution of 1917 ended this era. The Soviet state closed missions, executed or imprisoned clergy and cut off overseas dioceses, which reorganised as the Metropolia in North America (later the Orthodox Church in America), the Japanese church and the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia. After 1991 the Moscow Patriarchate rebuilt dioceses, translated scripture into minority languages and created a Synodal Missionary Department (1995), while supporting the 1997 law restricting 'non-traditional' religions and opposing Western Protestant mission in Russia as proselytism. Its close alignment with the state, including support for the war in Ukraine framed by 'Russian world' ideology, has been sharply criticised by other Orthodox theologians.
beliefs: Eastern Orthodox faith and worship as the fullness of Christianity, with the Byzantine-Slavonic liturgy at the centre of mission.
The Cyrillo-Methodian principle that peoples should worship in their own language, revived by Stephen of Perm, Ilminsky, Innocent and Nicholas.
Symphony of church and state: the tsar as protector of Orthodoxy and conversion as integration into the Russian realm.
Baptism as entry into both the church and imperial society, with apostasy treated as a crime until 1905.
Monastic holiness and the 'elder' tradition as the source of missionary vocation (Sergius of Radonezh, Valaam, Optina).
strategies: Creation of alphabets and translations: Old Permic for Komi, Cyrillic scripts for Volga and Siberian languages, Aleut and Tlingit writing.
State incentives for converts – tax and conscription exemptions – and penalties for apostasy and for proselytising by other faiths.
Destruction of sacred groves, idols and mosques and their replacement with churches.
Native-language schools and the training of indigenous teachers and priests (Ilminsky system, Alaskan readers, Japanese catechists).
Missions attached to trading companies and military outposts (Russian-American Company, Siberian forts).
Monastic settlements as centres of instruction and charity, such as Herman's Spruce Island and Glukharev's Altai mission.
groupsReached: Komi (Zyrians) and other Finnic peoples of the Russian north.
Volga Tatars, Chuvash, Mari, Udmurt and Mordvins after the conquest of Kazan.
Khanty, Mansi, Yakut (Sakha), Buryat and Altaian peoples of Siberia.
Aleuts, Alutiiq, Yupik and Tlingit of Alaska.
Japanese, especially in Hakodate, Tokyo and northern Honshu.
Albazinian descendants and some Han Chinese in Beijing; Koreans after 1900.
challenges: Resistance of Muslim Tatars and Bashkirs, and widespread return to Islam or traditional religion after nominal baptism.
Huge distances and shortage of clergy who knew local languages.
Conflict between missionary ideals and state or commercial interests (Russian-American Company, settlers).
Russian nationalist opposition to non-Russian-language liturgy.
After 1867 in Alaska, competition with American Protestant missions and English-only schooling.
Soviet persecution after 1917, which destroyed most missionary institutions.
harms: Conversion was frequently coerced or bought: tax and conscription exemptions for converts, criminal penalties for apostasy and pressure on whole villages produced nominal Christians.
Hundreds of mosques in the Kazan region were destroyed in the 1740s, and Muslim Tatars faced restrictions designed to promote conversion.
Sacred sites, images and groves of Komi, Khanty, Mansi and other peoples were burned or cut down by missionaries, from Stephen of Perm to Filofei of Tobolsk.
Mission in Alaska depended on the Russian-American Company, which exploited Aleut and Alutiiq hunters through forced labour and hostage-taking.
Missions often served Russification and imperial control, even when using native languages.
In the post-Soviet period the church has supported legal restrictions on other religions and aligned itself with state nationalism and the war against Ukraine.
developments: First alphabets and books for many peoples of Russia and Alaska, including Komi, Aleut, Chuvash and Mari.
A self-governing Japanese Orthodox Church with Japanese clergy and liturgy.
Orthodoxy as a lasting element of Alaska Native identity, and the Orthodox Church in America.
Ilminsky's mother-tongue schooling, which shaped later Soviet language policy and national literatures.
Saints – Stephen of Perm, Herman and Innocent of Alaska, Nicholas of Japan – who model a respectful, linguistically engaged mission within Orthodoxy.
missions.outcome: Russian Orthodox mission made Orthodoxy the faith of many Finnic, Volga, Siberian and Alaskan peoples and planted lasting churches in Japan and North America, but its dependence on imperial power meant that many conversions were nominal and that Islam and indigenous religions revived whenever coercion lifted. Its most enduring fruits came where missionaries translated, educated and handed leadership to local Christians.

agreements.text: Stephen of Perm, Ilminsky and Innocent all explicitly invoked Cyril and Methodius in creating alphabets and vernacular liturgy.
Shared commitment to scripture in minority languages; the Russian Bible Society (1812–1826) translated into several languages of the empire before Orthodox opposition closed it.
The Russian Orthodox Church joined the World Council of Churches in 1961, and Orthodox theologians contributed to ecumenical mission thought on liturgy and witness.

disagreements.text: After 1991 the Moscow Patriarchate condemned Western evangelical missions in Russia as 'proselytism' on canonical Orthodox territory and backed the 1997 law restricting them.
Pentecostal and charismatic churches growing in Russia and Ukraine are treated by the Patriarchate as sects, and have faced legal restrictions and harassment.

deviations: The Cyrillo-Methodian ideal of persuasion in one's own tongue was repeatedly displaced by state-backed coercion and material inducements.
Mission became tied to Russification and imperial expansion, at odds with Orthodoxy's own teaching that the church transcends nations (condemned as 'phyletism' in 1872).
Recent alignment of the Moscow Patriarchate with state ideology has been criticised by Orthodox theologians in the 2022 Declaration on the 'Russian World' teaching.
